title: A Hyderabad-Born Billionaire Bets $1 Billion on India — and May Finally Buy IDBI Bank
excerpt: Prem Watsa's Fairfax Financial parked nearly $1 billion in Indian bonds in a single week, signaling the four-year IDBI privatisation saga is nearing a close
body:
Canada's Fairfax Financial Holdings has parked nearly $1 billion in Indian government bonds — a rare, aggressive capital deployment that signals the long-stalled privatisation of IDBI Bank may finally be heading toward a close.

According to five sources cited by Reuters, Fairfax India Holding Corp, the Toronto-listed vehicle controlled by Indian-Canadian billionaire Prem Watsa, bought around ₹6,000 crore ($633 million) of the 6.03 percent 2029 government bond at an auction last week, at a yield five basis points below market levels. It also picked up roughly ₹600 crore of a 2027 bond and ₹2,600 crore of short-dated Treasury bills — bringing the total to approximately $1 billion in a single week.

The purchases, sources say, were structured to bring capital into India ahead of a potential deal to acquire a controlling stake in IDBI Bank from the government and Life Insurance Corporation of India. India's recent decision to exempt foreign investors in government bonds from capital gains tax made the transaction viable.

## A deal four years in the making

The government first announced the sale of its combined 60.72 percent stake in IDBI Bank in October 2022. The process crawled through expressions of interest, RBI "fit and proper" clearances, and finally financial bids — only to stall earlier this year when both Fairfax and Emirates NBD submitted offers below the government's reserve price.

Now, a *Moneycontrol* report suggests Fairfax has submitted a revised all-cash bid, proposing to make IDBI Bank the anchor of its Indian financial services empire. The deal, if concluded, could fetch approximately ₹50,000 crore (just over $5 billion) for the government and LIC combined. Fairfax is reported to have bid around ₹77 per share — a discount to IDBI's recent market close of ₹86.95, but one the government may now be willing to accept after years of delay.

"The revised proposal is under review, and the deal seems to be headed in the right direction," a source told *Moneycontrol*. A timeline of September 2026 has been floated, though nothing is confirmed.

## Watsa's Indian empire

Prem Watsa, born in Hyderabad and raised in India before emigrating to Canada, has built Fairfax Financial into a $25 billion insurance-and-investment conglomerate often called "Canada's Berkshire Hathaway." His India strategy has been unmistakable: Fairfax already holds a controlling stake in CSB Bank (formerly Catholic Syrian Bank, acquired in 2018), majority control of GoDigit General Insurance (a digital-first insurer co-founded with former Allianz CEO Kamlesh Goyal), and a growing position in IIFL Capital Services, where a ₹2,000 crore equity infusion in May lifted Fairfax's stake to 51 percent.

Under the proposed IDBI structure, GoDigit and IIFL Capital would be folded into IDBI Bank as subsidiaries, creating a unified financial services platform spanning banking, insurance, and wealth management. Fairfax has committed to divesting its 40 percent stake in CSB Bank to comply with the RBI's single-banking-licence rule.

The ambition is clear: IDBI, with its 1,884 branches and government-bank pedigree, would give Watsa's group a scale that CSB — a far smaller, Kerala-based lender — never could.

## What it means for the diaspora

For NRI investors, the deal tests a question that has hung over Indian markets since the Modi government's first disinvestment push: can India actually privatise a major public-sector bank?

If the IDBI sale closes, it would be the largest foreign direct investment in an Indian bank in history, and a proof-of-concept for future privatisations that the market has priced in sceptically for years. IDBI's shares, despite a market cap of ₹93,500 crore, still trade below their price of 13 years ago — a reminder of the asset-quality crisis that nearly destroyed the bank in 2018, when bad loans comprised a third of its book.

The bond-market maneuver is itself noteworthy for NRIs considering India fixed-income. Fairfax exploited the capital-gains tax exemption on government bonds — a policy designed specifically to attract foreign and diaspora capital — to pre-position nearly $1 billion at yields above six percent, in a currency that has stabilised as oil prices retreat. If the IDBI deal collapses, the bonds remain a solid investment; if it closes, the capital is already in-country.

For NRIs who recall IDBI as a development-finance institution their parents' generation trusted, the Watsa bid carries a particular resonance: a Hyderabad-born investor returning home to buy one of the institutions that once funded India's industrial backbone.

---

*Sources: Reuters, Outlook Business, Moneycontrol, Fairfax Financial filings*
